Central Angles In Cube

GeometryAreaConstructions
Game: This is a picture, not a game: it shows the angles you can make at the middle of a cube.
How to play: Drag P, Q and R onto corners of the cube, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Press Obtuse, Acute or Both to draw the rays, and use the other buttons to turn the cube.
Look for the math

Discussion by Scott E. Brodie on the original page. Join the middle of a cube to two corners and you get a central angle. Only two different answers are possible when the corners sit on the cube, and one is the exact complement of the other.

Two angles at the middle

Name the top face A, B, C, D and the face below it A', B', C', D', with each dashed letter directly under its plain one. Let O be the middle of the cube. The angle AOC goes from O to two opposite corners of one face, across a face diagonal: it is obtuse. The angle COC' goes to two corners joined by a cube edge: it is acute. The applet draws the first group with the "obtuse" checkbox and the second with "acute"; both boxes start unchecked, so the opening picture here also shows no rays. Press a button to draw them.

The cosine is a dot product

Put the cube of side 2 around the origin, as the page does, so A is (1, 1, 1) and C is (-1, -1, 1). The dot product of those two vectors is 1(-1) + 1(-1) + 1(1) = -1, while each has length sqrt(3). So cos(t) = -1/3 and t = arccos(-1/3) ≈ 109.47122°. For an edge, C·C' = 1 + 1 - 1 = 1, so cos(s) = 1/3 and s ≈ 70.52878°.

The page writes "arccos(s) = 1/3" where it means cos(s) = 1/3; the logic test checks both numbers directly, and they hold for every cube size it tries. This same angle is a building block of diamond and ice crystals.

Why the two angles make 180°

A and C' lie on a body diagonal, so the line AC' runs straight through O. Angle AOC plus angle COC' is therefore a straight angle: s + t = 180°. The page also looks at the right triangle ACC'. For a cube of side 2 its legs are 2 and 2 sqrt(2), its hypotenuse is 2 sqrt(3), and the middle of that hypotenuse is O. The line from C to O is a median of length sqrt(3), exactly half the hypotenuse. The test checks these lengths and the straight line at five cube sizes.

A tetrahedron hiding in the cube

Four alternate corners A, C, B' and D' form a regular tetrahedron. Every pair of its corners is a face diagonal of the cube, so all six angles at O are the same obtuse angle t; the logic test checks all six at every size. Press Show tetrahedron to see those four corners. The applet's "acute" group has one harmless quirk: the bytecode creates the ray OQ twice, so the second ray is drawn over the first rather than joining Q to R.

Press Both, then drag R onto the corner opposite P. The two numbers on the arcs always add to 180°.
